newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-ARMY AT WAR AS TWO CSKAS SEEK RUSSIAN LEAGUE SPOT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ARMY AT WAR AS TWO CSKAS SEEK RUSSIAN LEAGUE SPOT.

text.p: The Russian army has gone to war -- with itself -- after two rival professional soccer teams, both claiming to be the "real" CSKA Moscow, bid to represent the Army Central Sports Club in next season's premier league.

Vitaly Krechetov, general director of Russia's Professional Football League, told Reuters on Thursday his office had received two competing claims this week for CSKA's place in the 18-club top division. The season opens in March.

At the root of the problem is a fight between the army, which in its heyday turned CSKA into as fearsome a force on the sports field as the Red Army was on the battlefield, and Alexander Tarkhanov, who coached CSKA Moscow to fifth in the premier league last year.

Early this month, the army, in the shape of Colonel Alexander Baranovsky, head of all CSKA sporting activities, sacked Tarkhanov and replaced him with former Russian national coach Pavel Sadyrin, who had been fired by Zenit St Petersburg at the end of last season.

Now Tarkhanov, who is reported to have the backing of the Moscow businessman who owns 40 percent of CSKA soccer club, and Sadyrin, supported by the army, which still controls 60 percent of the shares, are training rival CSKA squads.
"We were not too surprised to see two applications from CSKA," Krechetov said. "They are at odds over who can legally represent the club and it is not for us to judge."
Ultimately, he said, it could go to court. Representatives of neither "CSKA" clubs were available for comment on Thursday.

The dispute over soccer is a replay of a monumental falling out at CSKA's ice hockey club. Colonel Baranovsky and the army appeared to come off worst in a clash with the legendary Viktor Tikhonov, who coached the world-beating Soviet hockey sides of the 1980s.

A series of legal battles has left Tikhonov in charge of the CSKA Moscow team which plays in the top Russian hockey league and in European competition. A separate CSKA team controlled by Baranovsky competes at a lower level.
The Army Central Sports Club is involved in more than 20 sports across Russia, including top flight soccer, ice hockey and basketball.

Soviet sport was largely run by big state institutions -- CSKA by the army, Dynamo by the police, Lokomotiv by the railways. The collapse of communism and privatisation of state assets has brought a host of squabbles over ownership.
For its part the Russian army, humiliated by lightly-armed rebels in Chechnya, is short of cash and a pale shadow of its former Soviet self.
